passages.t: All Israel gathers, and the Levite's account
passages.happening:
All Israel comes out, ‘from Dan to Beersheba and from the land of Gilead’, and gathers ‘as one man before the LORD at Mizpah’ (verse 1). Four hundred thousand armed men stand in the assembly of God's people (verse 2). They ask, “Tell us, how did this wicked thing happen?” (verse 3).

The Levite, ‘the husband of the murdered woman’, answers. He says the men of Gibeah surrounded the house at night. “They intended to kill me, but they abused my concubine, and she died” (verse 5). He tells how he cut her body in pieces and sent it through Israel, because they had done a shameful outrage in Israel. He asks for their verdict (verses 6-7).

All the people rise ‘as one man’ and swear that no one will go home until Gibeah is punished. They choose by lot who will fight and who will bring food for the army (verses 8-10). “So all the men of Israel gathered as one man, united against the city” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
For the first time in the book, all Israel acts together, from Dan in the far north to Beersheba in the far south, and Gilead east of the Jordan. The unity the judges could never bring about against foreign enemies is found only in a war against one of Israel's own tribes. The phrase ‘as one man’ comes three times. It is a unity in vengeance.

Mizpah in Benjamin, a few miles north of Jerusalem, was a traditional place for the tribes to gather. Samuel would later call Israel together there.

Listen closely to the Levite's account, because the reader knows what happened. He says the men of Gibeah meant to kill him. He says they abused his concubine and she died. He does not say that he pushed her out of the door to them. He does not say that he found her at dawn and told her to get up. His story makes him the victim and leaves out what he did. The narrator does not correct him. The reader is meant to notice.

The words he uses for the crime, outrage and lewdness, name a wrong against the whole moral order of the covenant. On that the nation agrees. The question the chapter raises is what the nation will do with its anger.

The numbers in this chapter are very large. Some scholars think the Hebrew word usually translated thousand can also mean a military unit or a clan's company, which would make the figures much smaller. Others take them as they stand, or as expressing the scale of the disaster.
passages.later:
The story of Achan shows an earlier time when all Israel acted together against wrong in its own camp (Joshua 7:24-25).

Samuel later called the people to Mizpah to repent: “Gather all Israel to Mizpah, and I will pray to the LORD on your behalf” (1 Samuel 7:5).
passages.asks: The Levite told the story so that he looked like the victim, and left out what he had done. Ask whether you have ever told a story about a wrong in a way that hid your own part in it. And ask what it says about a people that it could unite only in anger.

passages.happening:
The tribes send men through Benjamin. “Hand over the wicked men of Gibeah so we can put them to death and purge Israel of this evil” (verse 13). But Benjamin refuses. The Benjamites gather at Gibeah to fight the rest of Israel: twenty-six thousand swordsmen, and seven hundred chosen men of Gibeah, among them seven hundred left-handed men who could sling a stone at a hair and not miss (verses 13-16).

Israel goes up to Bethel and asks God, “Who of us shall go up first to fight against the Benjamites?” “Judah will be first,” the LORD replied (verse 18). The next day Benjamin cuts down twenty-two thousand men of Israel (verses 19-21).

Israel weeps before the LORD until evening and asks, “Should we again draw near for battle against our brothers the Benjamites?” The LORD says to go up (verse 23). On the second day Benjamin cuts down eighteen thousand more (verses 24-25).

Then all the people go up to Bethel, sit weeping before the LORD, fast until evening, and offer burnt offerings and peace offerings (verse 26). The ark of the covenant is there, and Phinehas, Aaron's grandson, serves before it (verses 27-28). They ask, “Should we again go out to battle against our brothers the Benjamites, or should we stop?” The LORD answered, “Fight, for tomorrow I will deliver them into your hand” (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
Israel's demand follows the law of Moses, which told Israel to purge evil from among the people. Benjamin's refusal put loyalty to its own tribe above justice. It shielded guilty men because they were its own.

The left-handed slingers of Benjamin recall Ehud, the left-handed judge from the same tribe, whose name meant son of the right hand.

Asking God, probably through the high priest, was the normal way to seek God's direction in war. The three questions grow more humble each time. First Israel asks only who should go first, not whether to fight. Then it weeps and asks whether to go again. Last it weeps, fasts, offers sacrifices, and asks whether to go or to stop. Only then does God promise victory.

The first question, and its answer, ‘Judah will be first’, repeat the opening of the book, when Israel asked who should go up first against the Canaanites. Now the enemy is Israel's own brother.

Phinehas was already a priest in the wilderness, in the time of Moses. His name here suggests that these events happened early in the period of the judges, within a generation or two of the entry into the land. That makes the depth of the corruption all the more striking.
passages.later: The law's command lies behind Israel's demand: “So you must purge the evil from among you” (Deuteronomy 17:7). Paul quotes that same law to the church, “Expel the wicked man from among you” (1 Corinthians 5:13), and the notes on that chapter explain that for the church the most it may do is put a person outside its fellowship, with the hope of bringing him back.
passages.hard:
If the LORD told Israel to go up to battle, why were they defeated twice?

The text records that the LORD answered Israel's questions, and yet forty thousand men fell in the first two battles. Readers explain this in several ways.

Some notice that Israel's first question asked only who should go first, not whether to fight at all, and that Israel went into battle sure of its own strength. The defeats humbled it, until at the third question it came weeping, fasting and offering sacrifice.

Others suggest that the defeats were a judgment on all Israel as well as on Benjamin, since the whole nation had drifted into the worship of idols and the moral chaos these last chapters show. The war was a disaster for every tribe.

Still others stress that God's word to go up did not promise an easy victory, and that the story shows the cost of a war among brothers.

The text does not explain directly. It lets the pattern of the questions and the suffering speak.
passages.asks: Benjamin protected guilty men because they were its own. Ask where loyalty to your group has pulled against justice, and which you chose. And notice that Israel came to God more humbly each time. Ask why God's people might need to be humbled even when their cause is just.

passages.t: The ambush, and a tribe nearly destroyed
passages.happening:
Israel sets an ambush around Gibeah (verse 29). On the third day Benjamin comes out again and begins to strike down men of Israel in the fields, thinking it is winning as before. Israel draws them away from the city (verses 30-32).

The men in ambush rush on Gibeah and put the whole city to the sword. A column of smoke rises from the city as the signal. The Benjamites look back, see their city burning, and are terrified, and Israel turns on them (verses 33-41). “The LORD defeated Benjamin in the presence of Israel” (verse 35).

Benjamin flees toward the wilderness. Eighteen thousand fall, then five thousand on the roads, then two thousand more. That day twenty-five thousand men of Benjamin fall (verses 42-46). Six hundred escape to the rock of Rimmon and stay there four months (verse 47).

Then the men of Israel turn on the rest of Benjamin. They put the towns to the sword, people and animals, and burn every town they come to (verse 48).
passages.hearers:
The ambush recalls the taking of Ai under Joshua, where Israel also drew the defenders out and burned the city behind them. The same tactics that once took a Canaanite town now destroy a town of Israel.

The battle is told twice, first in summary and then in detail, as Hebrew stories sometimes do. The totals differ slightly, 25,100 in one place and 25,000 in another, a common feature of ancient storytelling, which gives an exact count in one place and a round number in another.

The last verse is the most terrible. Israel does not stop with the guilty men of Gibeah, or with Benjamin's army. It turns on the towns of Benjamin, people and animals alike, and burns them. The punishment has gone far beyond the crime. A war that began to purge an evil has become a slaughter of Israel by Israel.

The book does not present this as justice done well. It presents it as the cost of a nation where everyone did what was right in his own eyes. Benjamin is nearly wiped out. Only six hundred men are left.
passages.later:
Israel used the same plan once before, at Ai: “Set up an ambush behind the city” (Joshua 8:2).

Hosea, centuries later, still remembered this war: “Since the days of Gibeah you have sinned, O Israel, and there you have remained. Did not the battle in Gibeah overtake the sons of iniquity?” (Hosea 10:9).
passages.asks: Israel's anger at a real wrong grew until it destroyed far more than the guilty. Ask where your own anger, even at something truly wrong, has gone past justice into punishing people who did not do it. And ask what limits you need around your anger before you act on it.
